extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, sociology, and general readers interested in democracy ( Tocqueville's Democracy in America )
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic prose arguing how equality of social conditions (democracy) transforms manners, social intercourse, compassion, class relations, and domestic service. The text draws contrasts between aristocratic and democratic societies, with frequent reference to American and European examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing aristocracy emerging from democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: As men become more equal and demand for manufactured commodities grows, wealthy, educated manufacturers open large establishments and by strict division of labor create a new kind of aristocracy arising from democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aristocracy applies exclusively to manufactures, contains some very opulent men and a multitude who are wretchedly poor, and differs from former aristocracies because its rich members have "no feelings or purposes in common, no mutual traditions or mutual hopes; there are therefore members, but no body." It is confined, unstable, and tends to use rather than govern the manufacturing population; it impoverishes and then abandons workmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic sympathy limited to one's own caste
rubrics_metrics.description: In an aristocratic community members of each class, considering themselves as children of the same family, cherish a constant and lively sympathy towards each other which is not felt to the same degree between different classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocratic ages produced strong intra-class bonds and duties (e.g., serf devotion to lords) grounded in social law rather than natural law; these ties produced generosity and self-devotion but not broad, cross-class sympathies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feudal/aristocratic institutions produce political obligations but not universal compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Feudal institutions awakened sympathy for the sufferings of certain men (members of one's caste) but engendered no real sympathies for humanity at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include chroniclers mourning nobles while ignoring massacres of commoners; heroic self-devotion within class combined with atrocities across classes. Such obligations arose from societal law/usage, not from a generalized sense of human solidarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of conditions softens public manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality of conditions and growing civility in manners are correlative facts: as social conditions tend toward equality, the manners of society are softened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ranks are similar, individuals can more readily judge and imagine the feelings of others, producing broader compassion and milder public behavior. The text treats this as a primary causal factor rather than merely contemporaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy broadens the range of human sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies, because all ranks think and feel similarly, each person can quickly enter into the sensations of others, so compassion extends over a far greater range of objects than in aristocratic times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument is that democratic equality makes it easy to 'cast a rapid glance upon himself' and thereby imagine others' sufferings; this increases humane acts (e.g., milder criminal justice in the United States) but does not eliminate specific injustices (e.g., slavery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity between nations mitigates cruelty between them
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion as nations become more like each other, they become reciprocally more compassionate and the law of nations is mitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Roman examples of extreme cruelty toward barbarians when Romans viewed them as not of the same human race; increased national resemblance reduces such barbarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy simplifies and eases habitual intercourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy places habitual intercourse on an easier footing; strangers meet with frankness rather than constrained deference because fixed social positions are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts English reserve (where rank remains important but ill-defined) with American frankness (where birth privileges never existed). Where social positions are uncertain (moneyed aristocracy), people avoid civilities for fear of social error; in truly democratic societies, exchange is natural and open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-defined moneyed aristocracy produces social reserve and hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: When aristocratic privilege is based on wealth rather than birth, social limits are ill-defined, producing secret hostilities, artifices to appear higher, and a general reserve (illustrated by English manners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because social position can be gained or lost by wealth, individuals fear intrusion or loss and therefore avoid easy intercourse; this explains anti-social tendencies attributed to the English in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: American openness due to lack of birth privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: In America, where birth privileges never existed and riches confer no peculiar rights, strangers are ready to frequent the same places and converse naturally, because they neither expect nor apprehend special obligations from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claim is used to explain the frank, open, and unpretending American manner; two Americans abroad recognize each other readily and are undeterred by social prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic temper: slow to take offense at home, sensitive abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans at home are slow to take offense and tolerant of minor breaches of etiquette, but when abroad they become excessively sensitive and punctilious about manners due to pride, uncertainty about social rank, and the desire to appear exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains this double effect: democratic familiarity at home reduces scruples, while American pride and ignorance of European status codes abroad make them anxious, scrupulous, and pretentious, often adopting exaggerated signs of wealth to distinguish themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy fosters mutual assistance and readily offered small services
rubrics_metrics.description: When men are equal and accustomed to frequent easy intercourse, they lend assistance to one another readily — small services and numerous modest donations are commonly rendered in democracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: spontaneous help after accidents, wide small donations after calamities; democracies produce continual minor mutual aids rather than grand acts of self-devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy produces a civic covenant of reciprocal, temporary support
rubrics_metrics.description: A tacit agreement exists between citizens of a democracy that each owes temporary support to others in times of common danger or weakness, similar to the professional solidarity seen among classes in aristocratic societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covenant is practical rather than passionate: people help if it requires slight sacrifice and often forget if help is unavailing, but the expectation of mutual aid is widespread and increases with equality of conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy alters master–servant relations and servile honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy does not eliminate masters and servants but changes their dispositions: servile honor and fixed hereditary servant lineages typical of aristocracies are weakened; servants in aristocracies may identify with masters and possess a 'servile honor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocratic societies create distinct servant communities with settled rules and pride tied to condition (e.g., 'soul of a lackey'); masters in aristocracies exert deep sway over servants' thoughts and habits. In democracies these stable class identities and ties are less lasting, modifying obedience, pride, and domestic relations.
